deep.reconstruction:
Context: Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792), Chapter 15, on divisors of sums of two squares. The page has three parts: (A) the end of a descent proof (§§557-561 together with §§550-556 on the previous page); (B) corollaries for primes 4n±1 (§§562-563); (C) an attempted 'more succinct' proof of the quotient lemma (§§564-568), which a marginal note refutes with a counterexample, followed by a summary (§569).

(A) §561, end of the descent. The setting is a coprime sum p^2+q^2 divisible by a number A that is not a sum of two squares. On the previous page Euler reduces p and q mod A to |p|,|q| <= A/2, so that p^2+q^2 <= A^2/2. The cofactor B = (p^2+q^2)/A then satisfies B <= A/2. By §556, which rests on the prime-divisor lemma §§551-554, either B or some factor of B is again not a sum of two squares. Iterating gives A > B > C > D > ..., an infinite descent of positive integers. That is absurd. Conclusion: a sum of two coprime squares has no divisor that is not itself a sum of two squares.

(B) §562. Let P = 4n+1 be prime. Then -1 is a quadratic residue mod P, so there is x with P | x^2+1. Here gcd(x,1)=1, so the sum is primitive. By §561 the divisor P is a sum of two squares (Fermat's two-square theorem).

§563. Numbers ≡ 3 (mod 4) are never sums of two squares, since squares are 0 or 1 (mod 4). Hence by §561 no such number divides a primitive sum p^2+q^2.

(C) §564. Euler seeks a shorter proof of the lemma: if N = a^2+b^2 divides p^2+q^2, then the quotient is a sum of two squares.

§565. Removing a common factor, one may take gcd(a,b)=1. Then gcd(N,a) = gcd(N,b) = 1, so a and b are invertible mod N. Hence any p, q can be written p = mN ± f a and q = nN ± g b (f ≡ ±p a^{-1}, g ≡ ±q b^{-1} mod N), in infinitely many ways.

§566. Since N | p^2+q^2, also N | f^2 a^2 + g^2 b^2. Euler then argues: 'because of the infinitely many resolutions, all cases making this divisible must occur, hence also g = f, since then the division works.'

§567. Granting g = f, take p = mN + f a and q = nN + f b (signs absorbed). Then
 p^2+q^2 = N( m^2 N + n^2 N + 2fma + 2fnb + f^2 ),
and Euler identifies the quotient as (f + ma + nb)^2 + (na - mb)^2.
My check: expanding gives f^2 + (m^2+n^2)(a^2+b^2) + 2f(ma+nb), as required.

§568. Corollary (contrapositive): if the quotient is not a sum of two squares, then neither is the divisor. Hence a product of a sum of two squares and a non-sum is never a sum of two squares.

§569. Combining with §558ff restates both conclusions:
- every divisor of a primitive sum of two squares is a sum of two squares;
- every prime 4n+1 is a sum of two squares.

Marginal note to §566. It doubts that g = f follows from divisibility, and gives a counterexample: a=7, b=4, N=65, p=17, q=6, p^2+q^2 = 325 = 5·65. There are no m, n, f with 17 = 65m ± 7f and simultaneously 6 = 65n ± 4f. My check: 7^{-1} ≡ 28 (mod 65), so f ≡ ±21. Then 4f ≡ ±19 (mod 65), never ±6. The note concludes 'haec posterior demonstratio rejicienda' (this second proof must be rejected). It adds that 325/65 = 5 = 1^2+2^2 even though 17 ≠ 1·7 ± 2·4 and 17 ≠ 2·7 ± 1·4. In other words, the representation 17^2+6^2 of 325 is not obtained by composing 7^2+4^2 with 1^2+2^2: those compositions give 15^2+10^2 and 1^2+18^2.
errors: §566 is a non sequitur. The existence of infinitely many representations p = mN ± fa, q = nN ± gb does not imply that g = f can be chosen. The case g=f requires p b ≡ ± q a (mod N).

The condition p b ≡ ± q a (mod N) does follow from N | p^2+q^2 when N is prime. Then (p/q)^2 ≡ -1 ≡ (a/b)^2, so p/q ≡ ± a/b, and §§564-567 is a valid proof for prime divisors. It fails for composite N. The marginal counterexample (N=65, p=17, q=6) correctly shows this, and the note rightly rejects the 'succinct' proof.

The statements of §564 and §568 are nevertheless true, but only via the full characterization (every prime ≡ 3 mod 4 occurs to an even power in a sum of two squares). Once the flawed lemma is removed, they are not established by the argument on this page.

Minor gap in the descent (§§558-561 with the previous page's marginal note). Reducing p,q mod A need not preserve coprimality. A common factor d of the reduced pair is coprime to A, so one may divide by d^2. This repair, done in E241, is not spelled out here.
§562 assumes without proof on this page that -1 is a quadratic residue mod a prime 4n+1. Euler proved this elsewhere.

results.what: Infinite descent: a primitive sum of two squares has only divisors that are sums of two squares (§561/§569)
results.modern_name: Euler's descent proof of the divisor theorem for x^2+y^2
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (letters to Goldbach 1747-1749; E241 written 1749, publ. 1752/53)

results.what: Every prime p ≡ 1 mod 4 is a sum of two squares, via -1 being a quadratic residue (§562)
results.usually_credited_to: Stated by Fermat 1640; first proof Euler 1747-1749

results.what: Numbers ≡ 3 mod 4 do not divide primitive sums of two squares (§563)
results.modern_name: Elementary consequence of the divisor theorem / -1 being a non-residue mod 4n+3

results.what: Attempted 'succinct' proof that (p^2+q^2)/(a^2+b^2) is a sum of two squares, writing p = mN+fa, q = nN+fb, with identity quotient = (f+ma+nb)^2+(na-mb)^2 (§§564-567)
results.modern_name: Brahmagupta-Fibonacci composition / quotient lemma; the proof is valid only for prime N
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (quotient lemma, E241); composition identity Diophantus/Brahmagupta/Fibonacci

results.what: Marginal counterexample N=65, p=17, q=6 showing the g=f step fails for composite divisors; 325 has three primitive representations, not all arising by composition with 7^2+4^2
results.modern_name: Non-uniqueness of representation for composite N (multiple ideal factorizations in Z[i])
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore; Euler's own work on multiple representations

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known descent proof of Fermat's two-square theorem, published in E241 and reproduced in the Tractatus. The only extra detail is an aborted alternative proof refuted by a correct marginal counterexample. It is a mildly interesting glimpse of self-correction but mathematically routine.

checkable.asserts: The §567 identity: p^2+q^2 = (a^2+b^2)((f+ma+nb)^2+(na-mb)^2) when p=mN+fa, q=nN+fb

checkable.sympy: all(sqrt_mod(-1, P) is not None for P in primerange(5, 2000) if P % 4 == 1)
checkable.asserts: -1 is a quadratic residue modulo every prime 4n+1 (used in §562)

checkable.sympy: all(any(isqrt(P-x*x)**2 == P-x*x for x in range(isqrt(P)+1)) for P in primerange(5, 5000) if P % 4 == 1)
checkable.asserts: Every prime ≡ 1 mod 4 (tested range) is a sum of two squares (§562)

transcription_corrections: The transcription is essentially faithful to the image. In §567 the image places '+ ff' outside the brace: (p^2+q^2)/(a^2+b^2) = {m^2(a^2+b^2) ± 2fma; n^2(a^2+b^2) ± 2fnb} + f^2. The transcription is consistent with this.
In the marginal note the image reads '17=1.7±2 4' (missing dot); it means 17 = 1·7 ± 2·4.
